how-to-calculate-pour-cost.html.text:
← Back to the pour cost calculator

How to calculate pour cost

Pour cost — also called liquor cost percentage — is ingredient cost divided by menu price, as a percentage. It answers one question: of every dollar a drink sells for, how much of it went to the bottle it came from? The rest of this page works through the formula on a real recipe, not a rounded example.

The formula

pour cost % = (ingredient cost of the drink ÷ menu price) × 100

Ingredient cost is the sum of every liquid poured into the glass. Each ingredient's cost is:

(bottle cost ÷ bottle size in ounces) × ounces used

Worked example

A margarita-style drink: 1.5oz of a $24 tequila (a 1L, 33.8oz bottle), 0.75oz of a $20 orange liqueur (a 750ml, 25.4oz bottle), and 1oz of lime juice from a $6, 32oz bottle — sold for $12.

IngredientCost / ozAmount usedCost
Tequila ($24 / 33.8oz)$0.711.5oz$1.07
Orange liqueur ($20 / 25.4oz)$0.790.75oz$0.59
Lime juice ($6 / 32oz)$0.191oz$0.19

Total ingredient cost: $1.84. At a $12 menu price, pour cost is $1.84 ÷ $12 = 15.4% — 4.6 points below a common 20% target, and not a problem: a drink running below target has margin room, not a mistake to fix. Priced to land exactly on a 20% target, this exact recipe would sell for $9.22 — so at $12 it is currently priced $2.78 above what the target alone requires. That number is a margin comparison, not a suggested price change; the market and your own menu decide what to actually charge.

What a small over-pour does to that number

Free-pouring the tequila a quarter-ounce heavy — 1.75oz instead of 1.5oz — adds about $0.18 to this one drink and moves its pour cost from 15.4% to 16.8%. That looks small at the register. At 200 of these drinks a week, it is $35.50 a week, or about $1,846 a year — liquor that left the bottle and never showed up as a cost or a margin anywhere the menu price could see it.

Common bottle sizes, for the cost-per-ounce step

BottleOunces
750ml25.4oz
1L33.8oz
1.75L (handle)59.2oz

Do this with your own recipes

The pour cost calculator runs this same arithmetic on your own bottle costs, pour sizes, and menu prices for a spirit-plus-modifier-plus-mixer recipe, sets your own target instead of assuming 20%, and adds the over-pour math above using your own drink volume. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

Checking one recipe by hand is a different job from tracking pour cost across a whole bar's inventory automatically — see how this free calculator compares to BinWise and WISK, two POS-integrated inventory platforms sold as ongoing subscriptions.

Common questions

What is the pour cost formula?

Pour cost percentage = ingredient cost of the drink ÷ menu price, times 100. The ingredient cost is the sum of every liquid that goes into the glass, each priced as (bottle cost ÷ bottle size in ounces) × ounces used. Nothing about labor, garnish, or overhead belongs in it — it is a liquor cost figure, not a full drink-cost figure.

How do I find the cost per ounce of a bottle?

Divide what the bottle actually cost (from the invoice, not a rounded guess) by its size in ounces. A 1L bottle is 33.8oz; a 750ml bottle is 25.4oz; a 1.75L handle is 59.2oz. A $24 bottle at 33.8oz costs about $0.71 an ounce, and that per-ounce figure is what every pour size gets multiplied by.

Is 20% pour cost good?

20% is a common target for spirits, but it is not a rule — it is a starting point you check your own recipes against. A drink running well under your target has room; a drink running well over it is being sold near or below what it costs once everything else the bar pays for is considered.

No warranty. This page and the calculator it links to are arithmetic references, not legal, tax, accounting, insurance, alcohol-service, or financial advice, and they do not tell you what to charge or how to run a beverage program. Verify every figure against your own invoices and a qualified professional before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

What does this drink actually cost you to pour?

A pour cost percentage from memory is a guess. Enter what the bottles actually cost and how much of each goes into the glass, and see the real liquor cost percentage against your own target — plus what a small over-pour on the well is quietly costing you across a year of shifts.

      Common questions

      What is pour cost?

      Pour cost — also called liquor cost or beverage cost percentage — is the cost of the ingredients in a drink, divided by what it sells for on the menu. A $9 drink that costs $1.80 to make has a 20% pour cost. It is the standard way a bar or restaurant beverage program checks whether a menu price is doing its job, the same way food cost percentage works for a kitchen.

      What is a good pour cost percentage for a bar?

      Most bars target somewhere in the 18–24% range for spirits, with beer and wine often run a little higher because they need less handling. There is no single correct number — it depends on rent, payroll, and how the rest of the menu is priced — so this tool lets you set your own target rather than assuming one, and shows you the gap between your target and what a specific recipe actually runs.

      Why does a small over-pour cost so much over a year?

      Because a single ticket hides the multiplication. A quarter-ounce over a 1.5oz pour looks generous rather than expensive on any one drink — it is a few cents. Multiplied by every well drink poured in a week, then by 52 weeks, a few cents becomes real, recoverable money that never shows up as a line item anywhere, because it left the bottle without ever touching a price on the menu.

      How is the target price calculated?

      It runs the same recipe cost backwards: recipe cost divided by your target pour cost percentage. It is not a suggested price — it is what this exact recipe, at this exact cost, would need to sell for to land exactly on the target you typed. The gap between that number and your actual menu price is the whole story: positive means the drink is priced above what the target alone requires, negative means it is priced below.

      Do I have to fill in a modifier and a mixer?

      No. The primary spirit is the only ingredient that is required — plenty of pours are spirit-and-mixer, or spirit alone. Leave a modifier or mixer’s three fields entirely blank to skip it. Filling in one or two of the three and leaving the rest blank is treated as an unfinished entry rather than a choice, so the form asks for the rest rather than silently dropping the ingredient.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Nothing about your bottle costs, recipes, menu prices, or drink counts is sent anywhere or stored anywhere but this device. If you use the save button, your recipe is written to this browser’s own local storage on this device only, and the forget button deletes it. The Copy shareable link button puts the same numbers in the page’s URL fragment, which your browser never sends to a server — nothing is uploaded that way either. The optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never any of your numbers.

      Is this alcohol-service, tax, or accounting advice?

      No. It is arithmetic on the bottle costs, pour sizes, and prices you type in. It has no opinion on responsible-service policy, pour-size law in your jurisdiction, staffing, tax treatment, or what to charge — check those against your own records, your state’s alcohol-control rules, and a qualified professional before acting on anything here.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Pour Cost Calculator

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet

A spreadsheet can subtract cost from price fine. Where it quietly goes wrong: a half-filled modifier or mixer priced as free instead of flagged, no way to solve backward from a target percentage to the price it needs, and no annualized figure for what a small over-pour costs across a year of shifts.

What each one actually does

A lot of beverage programs already reach for a spreadsheet: one column per ingredient cost, a formula that sums them, another that divides the total by the menu price. That arithmetic is trivial and a spreadsheet does it fine, for a recipe that is fully typed in. What it does not do on its own is catch the mistakes that actually change the number: a modifier or mixer line started but not finished, a target percentage that has to be reached by guessing at prices one at a time, and a small over-pour that never gets turned into what it costs across a real drink volume.

This calculator takes one recipe — a primary spirit plus an optional modifier and mixer, each priced by bottle cost, bottle size, and the amount poured — and works out the pour cost percentage, the price this exact recipe would need to hit a target you set, and the weekly and annual cost of a stated over-pour on the primary spirit across your own drink volume. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and nothing you type is uploaded.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What's this recipe's pour cost, given its ingredient costs and menu price?Either one — a spreadsheet divides fine, once every cost is entered.
I typed a modifier's bottle cost but forgot its pour size. What happens?This calculator — flags the unfinished line instead of quietly pricing it as free.
What price does this recipe need to hit an 20% pour cost target?This calculator — solves backward for the price in one pass, no trial and error.
What is a quarter-ounce over-pour on the well spirit actually costing across a year?This calculator's over-pour section — annualized from your own drinks-per-week figure.
How do I calculate pour cost by hand, with the formula and a worked example?This calculator's worked walkthrough.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?No, on either — but this calculator needs no formulas to build or maintain.

Most beverage programs get different value from each: an ongoing spreadsheet or POS export for tracking every recipe and every price change over a season, and a page like this one for an instant, no-login check on one recipe's real pour cost, the price it would take to hit a target, and what an over-pour on it is really costing before or without ever building a formula. This page's own figures are an arithmetic comparison built from what you typed in, not a substitute for your own cost records.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off. Nothing you type is uploaded.

A worked example

A well spirit at $22 a 750ml (25.4oz) bottle, poured at 1.5oz, mixed with 5oz from a $4 mixer bottle, sold at $7 with a 20% target: the recipe's real pour cost is 27.0%, 7.0 points above target, so hitting 20% at this exact recipe cost would take a menu price of $9.45, not $7.00. Nothing about that math needs a new spreadsheet formula — it needs the division run backward, which a cell built for the forward direction does not do on its own.

Add a quarter-ounce over-pour on the well spirit and the same recipe's pour cost moves to 30.1%. Across 400 drinks a week that is $86.61 a week, or about $4,504 a year, in liquor the $7 price never accounted for — a figure no single ticket, and no spreadsheet built one drink at a time, shows on its own.

Common questions

Isn't pour cost just ingredient cost divided by menu price?

That division is trivial and a spreadsheet does it fine once every ingredient cost is already in a cell. What a plain spreadsheet does not do on its own is decide what a half-entered modifier or mixer line means — a blank cell just computes as zero, which prices that ingredient as free rather than flagging that the entry is unfinished.

Why does a partially filled modifier or mixer line matter?

A recipe slot has three fields — bottle cost, bottle size, and the amount poured — and all three blank means the recipe genuinely skips that ingredient, which is a normal, valid entry. One or two filled in is different: it is a bottle cost typed in with no pour size next to it, which a spreadsheet formula either errors on or silently treats as zero. This calculator tells the two cases apart and asks you to finish or clear the slot instead of guessing which one you meant.

What does solving backward for the target price actually save you?

Most spreadsheets go one direction: type a menu price, get a pour cost percentage. Hitting a specific target percentage from there means typing a different price, checking the percentage, and typing again until it lands — trial and error with the same formula. This calculator solves the arithmetic in the other direction too: enter the target percentage and it shows the exact price this recipe, at its current ingredient cost, would need to hit it, in one pass.

Why does a small over-pour matter enough to compute a whole year of it?

A quarter-ounce over a 1.5oz pour looks generous on any single ticket, not expensive — a spreadsheet that only prices one drink at a time never shows the other side of it. Multiplied by the primary spirit's cost per ounce and the drinks actually poured in a week, then by 52 weeks, the same over-pour becomes a specific dollar figure across a year, which is the number that makes it worth fixing rather than shrugging at.

Does this replace a beverage program's own cost spreadsheet or POS reports?

No. A spreadsheet or POS report that tracks every recipe, every price change, and every ordering period over a season is still the right tool for that ongoing record. This page answers one recipe at a time — what its real pour cost is, what price it would need to hit a target, and what a stated over-pour on it is costing across a year — and nothing it computes is saved anywhere once you leave the page.

Open the Pour Cost Calculator to check your own recipe, or read how to calculate pour cost.

It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Verify every figure against your own invoices, POS reports, and accounts, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or pricing a menu with it. This calculator vs. BinWise

Two different shapes: BinWise links to your point-of-sale system and tracks pour cost automatically across your whole bar, under an ongoing subscription account. This page is a free, private worksheet for one recipe — its pour cost against your target, and what a small over-pour is quietly costing you across a year — with nothing to set up.

What each tool is for

BinWise is bar and beverage inventory software, sold under an ongoing subscription account to bars, restaurants, hotels, and restaurant groups running a full beverage program. It links to your point-of-sale system, updates inventory depletion in real time as drinks sell, and reports pour cost percentage and variance per product across your whole bar without anyone re-typing a recipe. Setting it up means an account, POS integration, and stocking your inventory into the system — not a one-off calculation. BinWise's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific plan names, feature tiers, or pricing, so only its well-documented category and identity are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This calculator does none of that. It does not link to a POS, track inventory depletion, or report variance across a bar's whole beverage program. It takes one recipe — a primary spirit plus an optional modifier and mixer, each with its own bottle cost and pour size — and works out the pour cost percentage against your own target, the menu price that exact recipe would need to hit it, and the weekly and annual cost of a stated over-pour on the primary spirit across your own drink volume. vs-wisk.html.text:
← Pour Cost Calculator

This calculator vs. WISK

Two different shapes: WISK is a paid, account-based platform for running a bar's whole inventory, purchasing, and POS-synced depletion tracking. This page is a free, private worksheet for one recipe at a time — what this drink costs to pour against your target, and what a stated over-pour is costing across a year of shifts — before you touch inventory software at all.

What each tool is for

WISK (wisk.ai) is inventory and cost-management software built specifically for bars, restaurants, and hotels with a beverage program. It connects to 60-plus POS systems to track depletion as drinks are rung in, uses invoice scanning and scheduled mobile physical counts to keep a running on-hand figure for every bottle across one or more locations, and runs ordering and purchase-order workflows on top of that count, all on a paid, ongoing account. It is a real, purpose-built platform for operational inventory control, not a pricing worksheet repurposed for it. Outbound requests to wisk.ai are blocked from this session, and independent software directories disagreed too widely on its current plan pricing (estimates ranged roughly $100 to over $700 a month depending on location count and feature tier) to state a representative figure here — check wisk.ai for its current plans.

This calculator does none of what WISK does. It has no POS connection, no physical count, no purchase orders, and no idea how many bottles are actually on your shelf. It takes one recipe's numbers — the bottle cost and pour size for a spirit, an optional modifier, and an optional mixer, the menu price, and your target pour cost — and prices that one drink, then shows what a stated over-pour on the primary spirit is costing across your own weekly drink volume over a year. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

When should I reorder a bottle, and what should the next purchase order be?WISK — built as an account-based platform with depletion tracking and purchasing for exactly that.
I run several locations and need one dashboard across all of them.WISK, or a comparable multi-location inventory platform — this calculator has no accounts and no concept of more than one recipe at a time.

The two are not substitutes, and a bar running a serious beverage program will likely want both. Knowing a recipe's pour cost and the annual cost of a small over-pour is a pricing and training question this calculator answers in seconds with nothing connected. Knowing exactly how many bottles are on the shelf right now, and when to reorder them, is an operational question that needs a live, POS-synced count — the job WISK is built for. A recipe can be priced exactly on target here and a bar can still be losing money to shrinkage or over-ordering that only an inventory platform would catch, and a bar can have tight inventory control and still be pricing a signature cocktail well under its own target because nobody ran the recipe math.

This calculator needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off. It has no inventory count because it is not trying to be one.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or WISK?

They solve different problems, and a bar running a full beverage program will likely end up wanting both. WISK is bar and restaurant inventory management software: it connects to your POS to track depletion, uses invoice scanning and scheduled physical counts to keep an on-hand inventory figure across every SKU and every location, and runs ordering and purchasing workflows, on a paid, ongoing account. This calculator does none of that. It has no inventory count, no POS connection, and no idea what is actually on your shelf. It takes the numbers for one recipe — bottle costs, pour sizes, menu price, and a target pour cost — and prices that one drink, then shows what a stated over-pour on the well is costing across a year of shifts at your own volume. An operator who wants to check one recipe's pricing or make the case for tightening a pour, right now, for free, with no signup, is in the right place here; one who wants continuous, POS-synced visibility into actual on-hand inventory and purchasing across a whole bar or multiple locations needs WISK or a comparable inventory platform.

Does this calculator track my actual bottle inventory the way WISK does?

No. This calculator has no inventory count, no POS integration, and no concept of how many bottles are actually on the shelf right now. You enter one recipe's bottle costs and pour sizes, and the calculator prices that recipe and checks a stated over-pour against your own drink volume. It does not know your depletion rate, your par levels, or when to reorder — that is what a dedicated platform like WISK is built for.
